opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a mistake to read those numbers as a verdict on the technology itself. Economic impact lags capability, sometimes by a lot. When you have a new general-purpose technology, the measurable effect on GDP or productivity depends on adoption: companies changing workflows, people learning to trust the tools, integration into real systems. All of that takes time, and it's much slower than the pace at which the models are improving.

From where I sit, the more relevant signal is what the models can actually do, and how quickly that's changing. If you look at a year or two ago, models were good at short, well-defined tasks: answering a question, writing a snippet of code. Now we're seeing them sustain much longer chains of reasoning, work on problems that take an expert hours, and act more autonomously. That trajectory hasn't flattened in any way I can see. If anything, the progress in reasoning has been quite surprising even to us.

So I'd separate two questions. One is "Is the technology getting more capable?" and I think the answer is clearly yes. The other is "Has the economy absorbed it yet?" and the answer is no, not mostly. A few percent of impact at this stage is roughly what you'd expect early in a transition like this. The really big effects, I think, come when these systems can do meaningful independent work, especially research, including research that accelerates the development of AI itself. That's a qualitatively different regime from a productivity tool, and I don't think the current economic numbers tell you much about when we get there.

If anything, I'd worry about the opposite failure mode: people looking at modest near-term statistics, concluding nothing dramatic is happening, and being unprepared when the capabilities translate into impact much faster than expected.

r001.rationale: The response says a few percent of impact is expected early in the transition and discusses capability progress, but it does not compare that impact with deep-learning NLP barely working roughly ten years earlier or frame it as remarkable progress by that comparison.

fable-5.1.text:
I think those numbers mostly tell you where we are in the adoption curve, not where we are in the capability curve, and it's really important to keep those two things separate.

When people look at a figure like three or five percent and say "see, it's not that big a deal," they're treating the economic measurement as a proxy for how good the models are. But the economy is enormous and it's slow. It takes years for a new general-purpose technology to show up in productivity statistics even when the technology is already in people's hands. There's a famous line about computers showing up everywhere except in the productivity numbers, and that lasted a long time before it reversed. So I would actually expect the measured impact to lag the underlying progress substantially, and I think we're seeing exactly that.

What I pay attention to is the trajectory of the models on hard problems. A couple of years ago, if you'd asked me whether a model could work through a difficult math problem for hours and come out with a correct proof, I'd have said that's some distance away. Now that's happening. The length of tasks these systems can carry out autonomously keeps growing, and that's the thing that determines economic value in the end, because most useful work is not a one-shot question, it's a long chain of reasoning and actions with a goal at the end.

So when I see those headlines I don't get discouraged, but I also don't dismiss them. They're measuring something real, which is that integrating this into organizations, into workflows, into regulation, is hard and takes time. What I'd push back on is the inference. The slow part right now is diffusion, not research. And if anything the gap between what the models can do and what the economy has absorbed is widening, which tells me the measured number is going to move a lot more than people expect, and probably not smoothly.

r001.rationale: The response says 3% or 5% measures adoption and argues economic impact lags model capability, but it does not compare that impact with deep-learning natural-language processing barely working roughly ten years earlier or frame the figure as remarkable progress on that basis.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s important to distinguish progress in the technology from its economic impact. A number like 3% or 5% doesn’t, by itself, tell you whether the underlying capabilities are improving more slowly. You’d need to know what’s being measured and over what period. And a few percent across an entire economy can be a very substantial change.

There’s also a gap between a system becoming capable of doing something and people reorganizing their work to take advantage of it. So I wouldn’t interpret those headlines alone as evidence that progress is slowing. I’d look at capabilities and adoption separately, and then ask how they’re translating into actual productivity.

r001.rationale: The response calls a few percent across the economy substantial, but does not compare it with deep-learning natural language processing barely working roughly ten years earlier.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we should be careful about what those numbers actually measure. Are we talking about an effect over a year, over a decade, or a change in the long-run growth rate? Three or five percent can be an enormous economic impact, and it doesn’t directly tell you whether progress in AI capabilities is slowing.

There’s also a gap between developing a capability and deploying it throughout the economy. Businesses need to change their workflows, build infrastructure, and figure out where these systems are useful. So I’d distinguish progress in the technology from the speed at which that progress shows up in economic statistics. They’re related, but they’re different questions.

r001.rationale: The response says a 3% or 5% impact could be enormous, but it does not compare that impact with deep-learning natural language processing barely working roughly ten years earlier.
